slides.title: Building a Modern C++ Application
keyPoints: Chapter 21
Building a Modern C++ Application
Modern C++ lecture with code, output, and presenter script
slides.narration: Welcome to Book II, Chapter 21: Building a Modern C++ Application. This deck follows the Chapter 1 Slides model: concept on the left, code or evidence on the right, and presenter notes that tell the instructor what to say and do. Modern C++ is not about using the newest syntax because it looks impressive. It is about encoding ownership, lifetime, invariants, generic behavior, and failure boundaries so the program is easier to reason about and harder to misuse.

slides.narration: The learning target is professional explanation. Learners should be able to say what Building a Modern C++ Application changes about program design, not merely identify a keyword. Push for three layers: the intent, the mechanism, and the evidence. In modern C++, the evidence might be a destructor running, a copy becoming independent, a move leaving ownership in exactly one place, a constrained template rejecting a bad call, or an algorithm producing a predictable sequence.

slides.title: 21.1 Designing the Ownership Model
keyPoints: The report owns its accepted task vector.
Parsing temporarily owns a candidate vector and a duplicate-ID index.
A successful load commits the candidate; a failed load leaves the previous accepted state unchanged.
This ownership model is the foundation of the application’s error guarantee.
slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 21, treat 21.1 Designing the Ownership Model as a design decision with costs and evidence. The report owns its accepted task vector. Parsing temporarily owns a candidate vector and a duplicate-ID index. A successful load commits the candidate; a failed load leaves the previous accepted state unchanged. This ownership model is the foundation of the application’s error guarantee. No global mutable collection or raw owning pointer is required. A graduate-level explanation should say what the abstraction buys, what rule keeps it honest, and what artifact proves the rule: source code, compiler acceptance or rejection, stdout, stderr, exit status, object state, or a test witness.

slides.title: 21.1.2 Avoiding Raw Owning Pointers
keyPoints: The entry point optionally owns an input file stream and otherwise uses standard input.
Its std::istream* is explicitly a borrowed selector between those existing streams, never a deletion owner.
The selected stream remains alive throughout loading.
The report follows Rule-of-Zero composition for its accepted storage.
slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 21, treat 21.1.2 Avoiding Raw Owning Pointers as a design decision with costs and evidence. The entry point optionally owns an input file stream and otherwise uses standard input. Its std::istream* is explicitly a borrowed selector between those existing streams, never a deletion owner. The selected stream remains alive throughout loading. The report follows Rule-of-Zero composition for its accepted storage. Temporary sets, vectors, strings, and streams clean themselves up through their library ownership. A bad allocation can still propagate rather than become a structured parse error, but the candidate-before-swap design prevents such a precommit failure from intentionally replacing the old accepted report. A graduate-level explanation should say what the abstraction buys, what rule keeps it honest, and what artifact proves the rule: source code, compiler acceptance or rejection, stdout, stderr, exit status, object state, or a test witness.

slides.title: 21.2.1 Combining Templates, Algorithms, and Ranges
keyPoints: The integer helper returns optional after complete from_chars consumption.
The line parser returns a variant containing either a valid task or an error string.
A set detects duplicate IDs, while a vector preserves the candidate task values.
These types expose different meanings rather than forcing every outcome into a sentinel integer.
slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 21, treat 21.2.1 Combining Templates, Algorithms, and Ranges as a design decision with costs and evidence. The integer helper returns optional after complete from_chars consumption. The line parser returns a variant containing either a valid task or an error string. A set detects duplicate IDs, while a vector preserves the candidate task values. These types expose different meanings rather than forcing every outcome into a sentinel integer. For output, a filter view selects open tasks from the accepted vector. Those tasks are copied into an owned report snapshot, then std::ranges::sort uses a tuple projection of priority and identifier. Priority one sorts before two and three; identifier provides deterministic tie-breaking. The owning snapshot can be reordered without mutating the accepted dataset. slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 21, treat 21.2.2 Using RAII Throughout the Application as a design decision with costs and evidence. Local owners make each exit path easier to review. If parsing fails, the candidate and duplicate-ID set are destroyed while the accepted report remains intact. On success, swapping the candidate vector with the accepted vector is the commit point, after which the temporary destroys the old state. The implementation checks input stream errors and the entry point checks output stream state after writing. It does not promise filesystem durability, bounded memory against hostile infinite lines, or a production-grade denial-of-service boundary. The per-line size limit is checked after getline has allocated the line, and the accepted row limit is ten thousand. These are teaching workload limits, not complete adversarial-ingestion protection. keyPoints: Read records in the form id|priority|done|title.

slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 21, treat Requirement and design as a design decision with costs and evidence. Read records in the form id|priority|done|title. IDs are positive and unique; priorities are one through three; done is zero or one; titles contain one to two hundred characters and no pipe delimiter. Reject malformed numeric fields, duplicate identifiers, invalid ranges, and over-limit training inputs. An empty file is a valid empty report. Blank lines are not silently skipped: they are invalid records under this grammar. On success, print the open-task count and total count, then open tasks ordered by priority and identifier. On a rejected load into an existing object, preserve the previous accepted state. slides.title: Follow one candidate to its commit point
keyPoints: Start with an accepted report containing ID 9.
Load a candidate containing valid IDs 1 and 2 followed by a duplicate ID 1.
The parser’s line buffer owns current text.
Temporary field views identify pieces of that text.
slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 21, treat Follow one candidate to its commit point as a design decision with costs and evidence. Start with an accepted report containing ID 9. Load a candidate containing valid IDs 1 and 2 followed by a duplicate ID 1. The parser’s line buffer owns current text. Temporary field views identify pieces of that text. Validated tasks copy titles into candidate ownership. The uniqueness set rejects the final ID before publication. The candidate’s destruction releases its strings, and ID 9 remains the accepted value. Run the same trace with a fully valid candidate. The final swap exchanges accepted and candidate storage. The old accepted vector now lives in the local candidate and is cleaned up when the function returns. No hand-written loop deletes old titles. The publication step is compact because the ownership model was designed before the update algorithm. slides.title: From the compact reference to the hardened extension
keyPoints: The original parser checks maximum line length after reading a line.
That is a limit on accepted input, not a bound on the line buffer’s peak allocation.
Appendix D changes the reader so it stops retaining bytes before the configured line limit is exceeded.
It consumes one excess byte to discover the violation and does not drain or rewind the remaining input.
slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 21, treat From the compact reference to the hardened extension as a design decision with costs and evidence. The original parser checks maximum line length after reading a line. That is a limit on accepted input, not a bound on the line buffer’s peak allocation. Appendix D changes the reader so it stops retaining bytes before the configured line limit is exceeded. It consumes one excess byte to discover the violation and does not drain or rewind the remaining input. The distinction is documented and tested at exact boundaries. The extension adds structured error codes and consistent line numbers. It accepts LF and CRLF records under a declared policy, accepts a final record without a newline, rejects blank lines, and treats an empty file as a successful empty replacement. It uses a fixed ASCII title policy rather than implying support for every Unicode text-processing requirement. An internationalized application would need an explicit encoding and character-policy revision. A graduate-level explanation should say what the abstraction buys, what rule keeps it honest, and what artifact proves the rule: source code, compiler acceptance or rejection, stdout, stderr, exit status, object state, or a test witness.

slides.title: Separate three recovery questions
keyPoints: After a failed load, ask whether accepted tasks changed.
Then ask where the input stream is positioned and which state bits are set.
Finally, ask whether any diagnostics or output bytes were published.
The answers can differ.
slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 21, treat Separate three recovery questions as a design decision with costs and evidence. After a failed load, ask whether accepted tasks changed. Then ask where the input stream is positioned and which state bits are set. Finally, ask whether any diagnostics or output bytes were published. The answers can differ. A strong accepted-state guarantee can coexist with consumed input and emitted diagnostics. A runbook for a caller should say whether to retry with a fresh stream, preserve the old report, or ask the user to correct the source. After a failed write, accepted tasks still exist, but the output sink may contain a prefix. Retrying to the same sink can duplicate that prefix. A file-publication adapter might use a separately validated temporary-file protocol; a message broker might use an application-level identifier and acknowledgement scheme. Those are different external contracts, intentionally outside this portable in-memory capstone. A graduate-level explanation should say what the abstraction buys, what rule keeps it honest, and what artifact proves the rule: source code, compiler acceptance or rejection, stdout, stderr, exit status, object state, or a test witness.

slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 21, treat Practice and implementation lab as a design decision with costs and evidence. Add fixtures for missing fields, an extra delimiter, invalid done values, negative IDs, leading numeric whitespace, duplicate IDs late in a file, and titles at both length boundaries. Do not label the training row limit a complete security control. Identify which guarantees are local language/library properties and which require a platform or deployment design.
